what_its_for: Risdiplam is used to treat spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in adults and children 2 months of age and older. SMA is a genetic disease that weakens the muscles needed for breathing, swallowing, and movement. This medicine helps your body make more of a protein called SMN, which is needed to keep nerve cells healthy and muscles working.
how_to_take: Risdiplam comes as a liquid that you take by mouth once a day. Always take it right after a meal, at the same time each day. If you use a feeding tube, your healthcare team will show you how to give it through the tube. Use only the oral syringe that comes with your medicine to measure your dose. Do not mix it with food or liquid. Swallow it right away after measuring — do not save it in the syringe for later.
dosing: Your dose is based on your age and weight and will be calculated by your doctor. Never change your dose on your own. For babies 2 to less than 12 months old, the usual dose is 0.15 mg per kg of body weight once daily. For patients 1 year and older weighing less than 20 kg, the dose is 0.2 mg per kg once daily. For patients 1 year and older weighing 20 kg or more, the standard adult dose is 5 mg once daily. Your pharmacist will prepare the right concentration for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still within 6 hours of your normal dosing time. If more than 6 hours have passed, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular scheduled time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store the bottle in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Once your pharmacist prepares the liquid, it can be used for up to 64 days when kept in the refrigerator. Write the date you first opened or received the bottle on the label. Keep it away from children. Throw away any unused medicine after 64 days or on the expiration date, whichever comes first.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, including vitamins and herbal supplements, because risdiplam can interact with some medications. Avoid taking medicines that are broken down by a liver enzyme called CYP3A without checking with your doctor first — examples include certain antibiotics, antifungals, and seizure medicines. Women of childbearing age should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men should use condoms during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: a skin rash or severe skin reaction; mouth sores or ulcers; eye problems such as redness, pain, or changes in vision; fever or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; or any signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Risdiplam starts working in the body fairly quickly, but you may not notice improvements in muscle strength or function right away. Some patients and caregivers report seeing changes within a few months, while for others it may take longer. It is very important to keep taking this medicine every day even if you do not feel different at first. Stopping treatment can allow the disease to get worse.
special_populations: Children under 2 months of age: Safety and effectiveness have not been established, so this medicine is not recommended for newborns younger than 2 months. Pregnancy: Risdiplam may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use reliable birth control during treatment and for 1 month after stopping. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if risdiplam passes into breast milk. Do not breastfeed while using this medicine. Kidney or liver problems: If you have significant kidney or liver disease, tell your doctor, as your dose may need to be adjusted or monitored more carefully. Elderly patients: There is limited data in older adults, so your doctor will monitor you closely.
